justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly upward-drifting baseline from an assumed current price around 120–121. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 121.2 is essentially anchored to the last known price with minimal drift, since over such a short window mean-reversion and momentum effects tend to cancel out and the most likely outcome is close to where the asset already trades. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 122.0, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with longer-run trend momentum without any specific near-term catalyst. At the one-month horizon, the 123.5 estimate extrapolates that same gentle drift further out, compounding the weekly assumption while acknowledging that one month is long enough for fundamental repricing to begin asserting itself.

The confidence interval widths widen dramatically as the horizon extends, which reflects the square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty that is standard in financial forecasting. At one day, realized volatility is the dominant input, and the relatively tight 118.5–123.9 band (roughly ±2.2%) reflects typical daily-to-intraday volatility for a moderately liquid asset. At one week, the band widens to 116–128 (roughly ±5%), capturing the accumulation of daily shocks and the possibility of a macro data release or earnings event. At one month, the 110–137 range (roughly ±11%) reflects the full range of plausible macro regimes, sentiment shifts, and idiosyncratic developments that can materialize over four weeks.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside even these widened intervals. On the upside, a surprise positive catalyst — such as a blowout earnings report, an unexpected central bank pivot toward easing, or a major positive regulatory development — could drive a sharp gap higher that breaks through the 137 ceiling. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macro conditions, a liquidity shock, or negative sector-specific news could push prices well below 110 within the month.

It is also worth noting that these intervals assume roughly normal return distributions with fat tails only modestly accounted for. True financial return distributions have heavier tails than a Gaussian model implies, so extreme moves — say a 15–20% shock in either direction within a month — are more probable in reality than the stated 90% confidence interval formally allows. Geopolitical shocks, flash crashes, or contagion from correlated asset classes represent the hardest-to-quantify tail risks that could invalidate even the widest stated bounds.
